passages.text: And I said, “Then are the things said by poets and philosophers correct: that in Hades the souls of the impious, after being judged for what they dared to do, are punished—such as the souls of Ixion, Tantalus, Tityus, Sisyphus, the daughters of Danaus, and all the others who ever acted impiously here? And if these things are not so, how could magic have any reality?” When he said that matters in Hades were indeed so, I asked, “Why, then, have we ourselves not feared magic, since we are convinced of the punishment in Hades for adultery? For I do not agree that it is right to use magic to force a woman who is unwilling. But if someone promises to persuade her, I am quite ready for that and to acknowledge my gratitude as well.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: how could magic have any reality
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑφεστάναι has an existential sense here: magic could not subsist or be real if the premises about Hades were false.

lexical_decisions.chosen: have we ourselves not feared magic
lexical_decisions.rationale: The first-person plural is retained as an inclusive rhetorical question; αὐτοί adds emphasis, ‘we ourselves.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπὶ μοιχείας πεπεισμένοι τὴν ἐν ᾅδου δίκην
lexical_decisions.chosen: since we are convinced of the punishment in Hades for adultery
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπὶ μοιχείας identifies adultery as the ground for the punishment; πεπεισμένοι governs the conviction expressed by τὴν ... δίκην.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρὸς τοῦτο μετὰ τοῦ καὶ χάριν ὁμολογεῖν ἑτοίμως ἔχω
lexical_decisions.chosen: I am quite ready for that and to acknowledge my gratitude as well
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἑτοίμως ἔχω expresses readiness, while χάριν ὁμολογεῖν means to acknowledge gratitude or indebtedness.

passages.text: And Appion said, “Do you not think it amounts to the same thing whether you obtain her by magic or by persuading her with words?” I said, “They are not at all alike; each is far removed from the other. The man who compels an unwilling woman by magic’s force incurs the harshest punishment as one who has schemed against a chaste woman. But the man who persuades her by speech and makes his appeal depend on her own freedom and choice has used no force. Still, I think the persuader will be punished less than the man who used force. So if you can persuade her, I will be grateful if I succeed; otherwise, I would rather die than forcibly compel a woman who does not consent.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: you obtain her
lexical_decisions.rationale: With a person as the genitive object in this erotic context, ἐπιτυγχάνω means to attain or succeed in obtaining that person.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπὶ τῇ αὐτῆς ἐξουσίᾳ καὶ βουλῇ ποιησάμενος τὴν παράφασιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: makes his appeal depend on her own freedom and choice
lexical_decisions.rationale: παράφασις can denote an appeal, exhortation, or persuasion. The ἐπί phrase makes her own authority and will the basis on which the appeal succeeds; the defensible alternative ‘makes the persuasion subject to her own freedom and will’ has the same contrast with force.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἧττον δὲ οἶμαι κολασθήσεσθαι τὸν πεπεικότα τοῦ βιασαμένου
lexical_decisions.chosen: I think the persuader will be punished less than the man who used force
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive τοῦ βιασαμένου supplies the standard of comparison after ἧττον.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I will be grateful if I succeed
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally, the speaker will ‘have gratitude’ upon succeeding; English expresses this naturally as being grateful.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I would rather die than
lexical_decisions.rationale: The comparative wording is emphatic in Greek; idiomatic English expresses the preference with ‘rather ... than.’

passages.text: And Appion, genuinely at a loss, said, “What am I to say to you? At one moment, as a man tormented by love, you wish to obtain her; at another, as if you were not in love, you put fear before desire. You imagine that after persuading her you will be free from liability as though sinless, but that if you obtain her by the force of magic, you will incur punishment. Yet you fail to understand that what is judged in every action is its outcome—the fact that it happened—not how it happened. And if you commit adultery, surely you will not be judged to have acted impiously if you manage it by magic, yet be absolved of the sin involved in adultery if you persuade her.” I said, “Because I am in love, obtaining the woman I love is in any case my settled aim. I must therefore choose one of the two, and, if possible, I will choose to flatter rather than use magic. But it is not easy to persuade her even with flattery, for the woman is thoroughly a philosopher.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: genuinely at a loss
lexical_decisions.rationale: διαπορέω conveys serious perplexity or uncertainty about how to proceed.

lexical_decisions.chosen: you put fear before desire
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive marks the thing over which fear is preferred; ‘prefer fear to desire’ is an equivalent alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: you will be free from liability as though sinless
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀνεύθυνος means not liable or not accountable, while ὡς ἀναμάρτητος presents the supposed basis for that exemption.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ τέλος παντὸς πράγματος κρίνεται ὅτι γέγονεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: what is judged in every action is its outcome—the fact that it happened
lexical_decisions.rationale: τέλος denotes the resulting end or outcome. The following ὅτι γέγονεν clarifies that the occurrence itself, rather than its manner, is in view.

lexical_decisions.chosen: if you manage it by magic
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle δυνηθείς leaves the action implicit; the context supplies succeeding in the adultery through magic.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πάνυ γὰρ ἐστὶν ἡ γυνὴ φιλόσοφος
lexical_decisions.chosen: the woman is thoroughly a philosopher
lexical_decisions.rationale: πάνυ intensifies the predicate φιλόσοφος; ‘very much a philosopher’ is more literal but less idiomatic.

passages.text: And Appion said, “For that very reason I am more confident that I will be able to persuade her as you yourself wish, if indeed we can speak with her.” I answered, “Impossible.” Appion asked whether it was possible to write to her. I said, “That is possible.” Then Appion said, “Before this night is over, I will compose a book, an encomium to adultery. You will take it from me and send it on to her, and I hope that, once persuaded, she will consent.” Appion composed that book and gave it to me. It was about this book that I thought during this night, and at just the right time I was reminded that I had it among the other books I carry with me. After relating these things, I showed the book to those present and read it aloud when they wished to hear it. And then, after reading it, I said, “Gentlemen, this is the education of the Greeks, with a noble theme for sinning without fear.” The book ran as follows:

lexical_decisions.chosen: For that very reason I am more confident
lexical_decisions.rationale: Ταύτῃ is taken causally as referring to the woman’s being a philosopher. It could more formally be rendered ‘in this respect,’ but the causal connection is contextually stronger.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Before this night is over
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔτι with the temporal dative indicates that the composition will occur while the present night still lasts; ‘this very night’ is an equivalent alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: once persuaded, she will consent
lexical_decisions.rationale: συντίθεμαι here means to agree or consent to the proposed relationship.

lexical_decisions.chosen: at just the right time I was reminded that I had it
lexical_decisions.rationale: εὐκαίρως is taken with the act of being reminded. A possible alternative attachment is ‘I was reminded that I conveniently had it,’ but the temporal reading is more natural in context.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: σὺν ἄλλοις βιβλίοις οἷς μεθ’ ἑαυτοῦ ἐπιφέρομαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: among the other books I carry with me
lexical_decisions.rationale: The relative οἷς is understood by case attraction to βιβλίοις, and the reflexive phrase is interpreted contextually with the first-person verb.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the education of the Greeks
lexical_decisions.rationale: παιδεία may also mean Greek culture or intellectual formation; ‘education’ preserves the immediate connection with the philosophical book just read.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: γενναίαν ὑπόθεσιν ἔχουσα πρὸς τὸ ἀδεῶς ἐξαμαρτάνειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: with a noble theme for sinning without fear
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording is ironic: γενναίαν calls the book’s ὑπόθεσις ‘noble,’ while the purpose or tendency expressed by πρός is fearless wrongdoing.

source_issues.issue: The third-person reflexive ἑαυτοῦ occurs with the first-person verb ἐπιφέρομαι. Later Greek can extend ἑαυτοῦ beyond strict third-person reference, so the supplied wording remains intelligible as ‘with me’; the classically expected first-person reflexive would be ἐμαυτοῦ.

passages.text:
The Lover to His Beloved
(Anonymously, because of the laws originating from foolish people)

At the commands of Love—the oldest of all—for the sake of a child. I have learned that you devote yourself to philosophy and, for virtue’s sake, emulate the life of those who are superior. And who could be superior? The gods are superior to all, and philosophers to other human beings. For philosophers alone know which actions are evil or good by nature, and which, though they are not so, are regarded as such through the enactment of laws. Take, for example, the act called adultery: some have supposed it to be evil, although it is good in every respect, for it takes place at Love’s commands for the multiplication of life. Love is the oldest of all gods. For without Love no mingling or generation can take place—of elements, of gods, of human beings, of irrational animals, or of all the remaining things. Indeed, we are all instruments of Love. But the craftsman himself, working through us and present in the souls of every being that is generated, is Mind. Consequently, it is not of our own volition that we desire to do his will, but when we are commanded by him. And if, while desiring by his will, we attempt for the sake of so-called self-control to restrain our desire, how will we not commit the greatest acts of impiety by opposing the oldest of all gods and human beings?”

lexical_decisions.chosen: The Lover to His Beloved
lexical_decisions.rationale: The nominative sender and dative recipient form an epistolary heading. ἐρωμένη denotes the woman loved or desired.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀνωνύμως διὰ τοὺς ἐκ τῶν ἀνοήτων ἀνθρώπων νόμους
lexical_decisions.chosen: Anonymously, because of the laws originating from foolish people
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐκ marks the foolish people as the source of the laws; ‘because of the laws made by foolish people’ is an equivalent contextual rendering.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπιταγαῖς Ἔρωτος τοῦ πάντων πρεσβυτάτου παιδὸς χάριν
lexical_decisions.chosen: At the commands of Love—the oldest of all—for the sake of a child
lexical_decisions.rationale: Ἔρωτος naturally depends on ἐπιταγαῖς, τοῦ πάντων πρεσβυτάτου describes Love, and παιδὸς χάριν forms a separate postpositional phrase. An alternative attachment would take ‘the oldest child of all’ together, but that leaves the relation of ἐπιταγαῖς less clear and fits the subsequent description of Love as the oldest god less well.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τίνες δὲ ἂν εἶεν κρείττονες ἢ θεοὶ μὲν ἁπάντων, ἀνθρώπων δὲ οἱ φιλόσοφοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: And who could be superior? The gods are superior to all, and philosophers to other human beings
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitives can be read comparatively: gods surpass all and philosophers surpass humans. A partitive nuance, ‘the gods among all and philosophers among humans,’ is also possible; the main rendering makes the implied comparison explicit.

lexical_decisions.chosen: For philosophers alone know
lexical_decisions.rationale: The demonstrative most naturally resumes the immediately preceding philosophers, who possess the claimed philosophical discernment. It could grammatically encompass both gods and philosophers, but the argument is directed to the recipient’s philosophical learning.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ποῖα δὲ τῇ τῶν νόμων θέσει (οὐκ ὄντα) νομίζεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: which, though they are not so, are regarded as such through the enactment of laws
lexical_decisions.rationale: The omitted predicate is supplied from ‘evil or good’; the parenthetical οὐκ ὄντα denies that the actions possess by nature the qualities assigned by law.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς γὰρ τὴν τοῦ βίου πολυγονίαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: for the multiplication of life
lexical_decisions.rationale: πολυγονία denotes abundant generation or production of offspring. ‘For life’s abundant procreation’ is a more literal alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: of irrational animals
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἄλογος contrasts nonhuman animals as lacking reason; ‘non-rational living creatures’ is an equivalent alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: present in the souls of every being that is generated
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπιδημέω literally denotes residing, sojourning, or being present among; here it describes Mind’s presence in the souls of generated beings.

lexical_decisions.chosen: is Mind
lexical_decisions.rationale: νοῦς is capitalized because the passage identifies it as the craftsman operating through all beings; ‘intellect’ or lowercase ‘mind’ would preserve the lexical sense but less clearly convey the personified cosmic role.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ κελευσθῶμεν, τὸ ἐκείνου βούλημα
lexical_decisions.chosen: we are commanded by him ... his will
lexical_decisions.rationale: The pronouns immediately follow the identification of the craftsman as Mind, while the argument also closely identifies that craftsman with Love’s activity. The English preserves the masculine referent without forcing a sharper distinction between Love and Mind than the passage supplies.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: χάριν τῆς λεγομένης σωφροσύνης κρατεῖν τῆς ἐπιθυμίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: for the sake of so-called self-control to restrain our desire
lexical_decisions.rationale: σωφροσύνη can mean self-control, moderation, or chastity. ‘Self-control’ suits the immediately following attempt to master sexual desire, while ‘so-called chastity’ remains a viable context-specific alternative.
